initial_observation.encounter_context: referred to the Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery outpatient clinic at the Lauro Wanderley University Hospital, Federal University of Paraíba
initial_observation.chief_complaint: progressive development of edema in the right maxillofacial region
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: Patient presented with a swelling in the right maxillofacial region present for about a month, initially asymptomatic, which then developed into local discomfort and difficulty chewing. No history of trauma, local infections, or relevant systemic conditions. Ectoscopic evaluation showed significant facial asymmetry with bulging in the right maxillary region causing distortion of facial contour. Oroscopic exam revealed pronounced swelling in the posterior right maxilla with smooth surface, erythema, slight expansion of the hard palate, and mucosal hyperemia. No superficial ulcerations but internal bulging suggested an underlying expansive process.
presenting_symptoms: progressive edema in right maxillofacial region

evidence_items.source_text: In the ectoscopic evaluation, significant facial asymmetry was observed, with obvious bulging in the right maxillary region, causing a slight distortion of the facial contour (Fig. 1a and b). Oroscopic examination revealed a pronounced swelling in the posterior area of the right maxilla, with a smooth surface, erythema and slight expansion of the hard palate, as well as hyperemia of the mucosa (Fig. 1c and d). Intraoral inspection revealed no superficial ulcerations, but the internal bulging suggested an underlying expansive process.

Cone beam computed tomography was performed for a more detailed assessment. Figure 2a and b show an expansive mass affecting the posterior region of the right maxilla, extending to the base of the maxillary sinus. The lesion shows heterogeneous areas with varying density, suggesting mixed lytic and sclerotic components, characteristic of aggressive lesions. The presence of bone destruction is evident, with compromised bone margins and involvement of adjacent structures, indicating invasive behavior of the mass. The mass is also visible in Fig. 2c and d, causing alterations to the bone contour and invading adjacent tissues. Significant erosion of the right maxillary bone can be seen, with areas of mixed density. The irregular density of the tumor suggests the production of osteoid matrix. The extension of the lesion beyond the primary bone structures reinforces the aggressive and infiltrative nature of the lesion.
An incisional biopsy was carried out on an investigative basis due to the clinical and radiographic suspicion of malignancy found in the radiographic and clinical findings.

Immunohistochemistry showed a high proportion of positivity for Ki-67 (Fig. 3), suggesting aggressive behavior of the lesion. Other markers were used (beta-catenin, myogenin, pan-cytokeratin, U70, CD34 and desmin), but only CD34 was positive.

The absence of nuclear expression suggests that the Wnt/beta-catenin signaling pathway is not activated in this tumor, a relevant feature since nuclear translocation of beta-catenin is associated with certain types of neoplasms where this pathway is activated. Expression restricted to the cytoplasm also indicates that the tumor has histological characteristics that differentiate it from neoplasms in which nuclear beta-catenin plays a significant role in biological behavior. The CD34 marker showed prominent positive immunoreactivity in the endothelial cells lining the blood vessels in the tumor stroma. The presence of CD34 in blood vessels makes it possible to visualize the intratumoral vascular architecture, which shows a pattern of vascularization characteristic of tumours with high angiogenesis. The absence of staining in tumor cells indicates that this marker is limited to the vascular endothelium and does not suggest hematopoietic differentiation or other origins for the tumor. Ki-67 expression (Fig. 3) is markedly positive in a large number of cells, reflecting a high rate of cellular disruption in the tumor. This intense nuclear labeling is indicative of high mitotic activity, a common feature in high-grade neoplasms. The three slides confirmed the widespread presence of Ki-67, with a high proportion of marked cells, indicating that the tumor has a potential for aggressive and rapid growth. This marker therefore reinforces the tumor’s intense proliferative behavior. Desmin staining shows no immunoreactivity in the tumor cells, underlining the absence of muscle differentiation. Negativity for desmin indicates that the tumor is not related to smooth or skeletal muscle tissues, helping to exclude neoplasms such as leiomyosarcomas and rhabdomyosarcomas. Investigation for myogenin, a specific marker for skeletal muscle differentiation, showed no immunoreactivity in the tumor cells, highlighting the absence of differentiation to skeletal muscle. This absence is important for differential diagnosis, as neoplasms such as rhabdomyosarcoma would be positive for myogenin. The negativity of the tumor for this marker indicates that it does not have histological characteristics of muscle differentiation. Testing for pancytokeratin, a marker of epithelial differentiation, was negative in tumor cells. The absence of reactivity for cytokeratin suggests that the tumor does not have an epithelial origin, which helps to exclude carcinomas and other epithelium-derived tumors. Negativity for this marker indicates that the tumor cells did not have epithelial characteristics, reinforcing the hypothesis of a mesenchymal or non-epithelial tumor. Staining for smooth muscle actin (U70) showed no immunoreactivity in the tumor cells, indicating that the tumor does not show smooth muscle differentiation. The absence of muscle actin in the cells reinforces that the tumor does not have myoid characteristics, such as those seen in leiomyosarcomas or other smooth muscle tumors. This negativity is essential to avoid tumors with a muscular origin or differentiation.

After performing the incisional biopsy, which resulted in an initial analysis of the nature of the tumor and confirmation of the pathological entity, the definitive surgical procedures were planned and performed. The aim of this surgical approach was complete resection of the lesion, taking into account the extent of tumor invasion identified on imaging tests and confirmed by histopathological findings. The procedure included careful removal of the compromised tumor tissue, with a safety margin to reduce the risk of local recurrence (Fig. 4a and b), accompanied by removal of the affected area to restore functionality and aesthetics to the maxillofacial region. The surgical specimen was sent for further histopathological analysis (Fig. 4c).

The slides stained with hematoxylin and eosin (HE) (Fig. 6) show the classic characteristics of a small cell osteosarcoma lesion, as evidenced by the cellular and stromal pattern. There is an intense proliferation of small, round cells with a monotonous appearance, distributed in a dense and disorganized manner. These cells have a hyperchromatic nucleus and scarce cytoplasm, reinforcing the undifferentiated nature of the neoplasm. In addition, there are areas where the stroma is mineralized, with the presence of irregularly arranged bone matrix formation, a fundamental feature for the diagnosis of osteosarcoma, as it indicates direct production of osteoid matrix by the tumour cells. Another notable feature is the infiltrative aspect of the lesion, with tumor cells invading and breaking through the adjacent tissue architecture, without defined boundaries. This behavior suggests aggressiveness and is consistent with the malignant nature of osteosarcoma. Finally, areas of tumor necrosis and hemorrhage are present in some slides, demonstrating a rapid and disorganized growth pattern, typical of high-grade malignant bone tumors.

evidence_items.source_text: The immunohistochemical slides of beta-catenin (Fig. 5) show staining located predominantly in the cytoplasm of the tumor cells, with no evidence of nuclear translocation. The cytoplasmic expression of beta-catenin, with no nuclear presence, suggests the absence of activation of the Wnt/beta-catenin pathway, a relevant characteristic for the differential diagnosis of tumors where this pathway is not active. CD99, on the other hand, shows strong membrane expression in tumor cells. Membrane marking of CD99 is indicative of a characteristic profile in neoplasms that present this protein, and is a relevant finding for identifying lineage-specific or aggressive tumors. In the slide with desmin, there is no expression in the tumor cells, reducing the absence of muscle differentiation. This lack of expression is important in the differential diagnosis with myoid tumors, such as rhabdomyosarcomas, where desmin is normally expressed. The absence of desmin suggests an undifferentiated phenotype. Expression of S100 is negative in tumor cells, which excludes the possibility of a neural or melanocytic origin, characteristics in which the S100 protein is usually expressed. This finding is relevant for excluding tumors derived from neuroectodermal or melanocytic tissues, where the S100 marker would be present.

hidden_reference.final_diagnosis_verbatim: classic characteristics of a small cell osteosarcoma lesion, as evidenced by the cellular and stromal pattern ...indicates direct production of osteoid matrix by the tumour cells...characteristic profile...consistent with the malignant nature of osteosarcoma
diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: Histologically, SCOS is characterized by small cells with scarce cytoplasm, associated with osteoid production (Zhong et al. 2020). This lesion can be easily confused with Ewing’s sarcoma, malignant lymphoma and mesenchymal chondrosarcoma (Fletcher et al. 2013). The presence of calcifications in the intramedullary cavity or an extraosseous mass in soft tissues, reflecting the osteoid matrix produced by the tumor cells, is a frequently observed feature and helps in the differential diagnosis of SCOS in relation to other small cell tumors (Kilpatrick et al. 2018; Yarmish et al. 2010; Klein and Siegal 2006).

Immunohistochemistry showed a high proportion of positivity for Ki-67 (Fig. 3), suggesting aggressive behavior of the lesion. Other markers were used (beta-catenin, myogenin, pan-cytokeratin, U70, CD34 and desmin), but only CD34 was positive.

Another notable feature is the infiltrative aspect of the lesion, with tumor cells invading and breaking through the adjacent tissue architecture, without defined boundaries. This behavior suggests aggressiveness and is consistent with the malignant nature of osteosarcoma.

The immunohistochemical slides of beta-catenin (Fig. 5) show staining located predominantly in the cytoplasm of the tumor cells, with no evidence of nuclear translocation. CD99, on the other hand, shows strong membrane expression in tumor cells. In the slide with desmin, there is no expression in the tumor cells, reducing the absence of muscle differentiation.

In this case, immunohistochemistry was essential for a correct diagnosis (Tan et al. 2020). The analyses revealed negativity for markers common to other small cell neoplasms, such as CD99 and pancytokeratin, eliminating the diagnosis of Ewing’s sarcoma and undifferentiated carcinoma, respectively. In addition, negativity for muscle markers, such as desmin, also helped to rule out diagnoses of neoplasms of muscular origin. The expression of beta-catenin and the positivity of S-100 in specific areas reinforced the hypothesis of a tumor of bone and mesenchymal origin, thus confirming the diagnosis of osteosarcoma (Bishop et al. 2015; Kuo and Kent 2019).
